explanation: Use binary GCD. Order the arguments; remove common powers of two, discard a factor of two from just the even argument when the other is odd, and subtract the smaller odd argument from the larger. Stop when the smaller argument becomes zero.
timeComplexity: O(B) bounded-width arithmetic steps for B input bits: after at most a constant number of swaps/subtractions, an operand is halved. Big-integer bit costs are additional. Operand bit length decreases through Euclidean remainders or binary-GCD halving; big-integer arithmetic costs are separate.
spaceComplexity: O(B) recursive frames; no tail-call elimination is assumed. Iterative variants keep a constant number of integer values; recursive binary variants keep O(B) frames.
attribution: Unmodified reference from epi_judge_python_solutions/gcd.py; Elements of Programming Interviews Judge contributors; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International, retained in repository LICENSE. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: For even x,y, gcd(x,y)=2·gcd(x/2,y/2). If only one is even, halving that argument does not remove any common odd divisor. For two odd arguments, gcd(x,y)=gcd(x,y−x), after which the difference is even. These identities preserve the answer while shrinking the arguments, until gcd(0,y)=y.
walkthrough: For (84,30), halve both and remember a factor 2: solve (42,15). Reorder to (15,42), halve the even argument to (15,21), subtract to (15,6), reorder to (6,15), halve to (3,15), and subtract/halve until (0,3). Restore the saved factor 2, returning 6.
edgeCases: Use long arithmetic for the nonnegative input range.
